name: Cisco
product_focus: Catalyst SD-WAN, Meraki MX, Cisco Secure Access
evidence_summary: Cisco sources evidence SD-WAN Cloud OnRamp, Meraki SD-WAN, and SD-WAN + Secure Access SASE integration.
cost_model: Quote-based subscription/licence + appliance/support; Meraki public SKUs via partners, enterprise pricing varies by platform and term.
key_differentiators: Broadest platform portfolio in the category, covering Catalyst SD-WAN for enterprise WAN, Meraki MX for cloud-managed branch, and Cisco Secure Access for converged SASE delivery.
Cloud OnRamp provides automated optimisation paths for Microsoft 365, Salesforce, and major cloud providers, with native integration into the Cisco security stack.
Large global partner and integrator ecosystem reduces delivery risk for buyers wanting managed or co-managed delivery.
best_fit_for: Enterprises already standardised on Cisco networking who want platform consistency from LAN through WAN to security.
Multinational organisations needing strong vendor presence across regions and a deep partner channel.
Buyers prioritising single-vendor risk consolidation across networking and security.
watch_outs: Two distinct SD-WAN product lines (Catalyst and Meraki) means buyers should confirm which fits the target deployment profile and the longer-term roadmap.
Managed delivery is partner-led rather than first-party, so service quality varies meaningfully by integrator.
Private global backbone is not part of the platform; cloud transport relies on internet and partner gateways.
verification_notes: Re-verified 2026-07-29 against named primary sources. Every graded fact carries a source, a tier and a verbatim quote confirmed present on the cited page by an independent check. Industry, region, organisation-size and pricing evidence was sourced on the same basis. Facts that could not be sourced are published as unknown with the reason. The value_tier field is a Netify assessment of relative cost position, not a supplier claim: most of this market publishes no price. Sources found and rejected are listed at tier 4.

ai_capability.note: AI Assistant across Catalyst and Meraki dashboards; predictive path analytics; Talos-backed security AI.

resilience.note: Multi-region controllers, HA edge pairs and SSE redundancy via Cisco Secure Access.

profile.platform_architecture: Cisco offers two SD-WAN families. Catalyst SD-WAN (formerly Viptela) is the enterprise platform: vEdge and Catalyst 8000 routers, separated control and data planes, and vManage (now Catalyst SD-WAN Manager) for orchestration. Meraki is the cloud-managed alternative, with MX appliances configured entirely from the Meraki dashboard. Both integrate with Cisco's wider switching, wireless and identity portfolio, and cloud on-ramps cover AWS, Azure and Google Cloud. The two platforms remain distinct, so buyers should choose a track early.
profile.security_sase: Cisco's SASE position combines Cisco Secure Access (the successor to Umbrella for SSE), Duo for identity and device trust, and Talos threat intelligence. ZTNA, SWG, CASB and DLP are delivered from Cisco's cloud with single-console ambitions under Secure Access. On-box security on Catalyst and Meraki includes NGFW, IPS and content filtering. The strongest story is for Meraki estates pairing MX SD-WAN with Secure Access in a Cisco-only stack.
profile.service_support_channel: Cisco sells through the largest partner ecosystem in networking. Most buyers consume Catalyst SD-WAN through managed service providers, including BT, Verizon, Orange and NTT, while Meraki suits in-house teams and MSPs alike. Cisco TAC provides 24x7 follow-the-sun support; named technical account management comes via Cisco CX or the partner. UK channel depth is extensive at every tier.
profile.commercials_verdict: Licensing is subscription based: Cisco DNA/Catalyst licences per device tier plus Secure Access per user, with Meraki licences per appliance. List pricing is partially public via partners. The Netify verdict: shortlist Cisco when you already run Cisco switching, wireless or identity, when your operations team knows the tooling, or when you want one vendor across campus and WAN. Expect platform choice (Catalyst vs Meraki) to shape cost and operations more than headline pricing.

vendor_faqs.q: Should I choose Catalyst SD-WAN or Meraki SD-WAN?
vendor_faqs.a: Catalyst SD-WAN suits large, complex WANs needing granular routing control, segmentation and scale. Meraki suits lean IT teams and distributed estates that value dashboard simplicity over deep configurability. They are separate platforms with separate management, so pilot the operational model, not just the data sheet.

vendor_faqs.q: Does Cisco offer a full single-vendor SASE?
vendor_faqs.a: Yes in portfolio terms: SD-WAN (Catalyst or Meraki) plus Cisco Secure Access for SSE, with Duo identity and Talos intelligence. Policy and console unification has improved but is newer than rivals built single-stack from day one, so validate console workflows in a proof of concept.

vendor_faqs.q: How do most UK enterprises buy Cisco SD-WAN?
vendor_faqs.a: Through managed service providers and Cisco Gold partners. BT, Verizon, Orange, NTT and many UK MSPs run managed Catalyst and Meraki offers, which suits buyers who want carrier-grade delivery without operating vManage themselves.

shortlist_summary: Cisco offer the broadest platform portfolio in the category: Catalyst SD-WAN for enterprise WAN, Meraki MX for cloud-managed branch environments, and Cisco Secure Access for converged SASE delivery. Typically shortlisted by organisations with existing Cisco investments looking to extend rather than replace, though buyers should be specific about which Cisco platform they're evaluating as the architectures and operational models differ considerably.
cost_note: Subscription licensing; Meraki is mid, Catalyst total cost runs higher, so blended mid leaning premium.
uk_basis: No UK HQ (US). Extensive UK channel; Catalyst and Meraki widely delivered as UK managed services.

f01_fully_managed_service.quote: Create a multitude of offers from managed business Wi-Fi to managed SD-WAN
f01_fully_managed_service.note: Cisco positions itself as the technology platform that partners wrap a managed service around, rather than as the party that designs, deploys, monitors, changes and reports on the customer's service end to end. The Meraki managed services page addresses MSPs as the service operator. No Cisco-branded end-to-end fully managed SD-WAN or SASE service was found across the SD-WAN solution page, the SASE page or the Cisco Services page.

f03_co_managed_service.quote: Cisco Services and our network of partners act as an extension of your IT team.
f03_co_managed_service.note: Partial rather than yes. Cisco does run the Secure Access cloud platform and its support while the customer sets policy, which is structurally co-managed, and the services page describes an extension-of-your-team model. However no page reviewed sets out a named co-managed offer with a defined split of change rights and policy rights between Cisco and the customer. Graded low confidence because the quote is generic positioning rather than a description of a co-managed service construct.

f04_multi_tenant_msp_white_label_support.quote: Managed Service Providers (MSPs) can now take advantage of custom branding options within the Cisco Meraki Dashboard.
f04_multi_tenant_msp_white_label_support.note: All four elements of the definition are evidenced. Branded portals from the Meraki dashboard branding documentation, which also states "Any logos that are applied to Dashboard should be the logo of the MSP and not of the end customer." Tenant isolation and delegated administration from multi-organisation management, corroborated on the Secure Access datasheet: "Large enterprise customers can manage multiple organizations (orgs) through a single user interface, with central access and license management." Branding is configured per organisation and can be cloned to new organisations as a template.

f05_professional_services_and_migration_.quote: Cisco Professional Services provide strategic consulting, design, and implementation expertise to help you build or transform your IT environment.
f05_professional_services_and_migration_.note: Partial because the definition is narrower than the label. Consulting, design and implementation are evidenced verbatim, but no page reviewed names the specific structured artefacts the definition requires: discovery workshops, pilots, staging, migration runbooks, rollback plans or training. Graded partial rather than yes on that gap, not on any doubt that Cisco has a large professional services arm.

f07_lifecycle_management.quote: Cisco Support focuses on software updates, hardware replacement, and rapid issue resolution to keep your operations running smoothly.
f07_lifecycle_management.note: Hardware replacement and software updates or patching are stated verbatim, and firmware upgrade automation is corroborated on the Meraki managed services page: "Use remote troubleshooting and automatic firmware updates to provide a superior service". Confidence is medium rather than high because renewals management and end-of-life planning were not found in the pages reviewed, and because Cisco support is normally a separately purchased contract rather than something inherently bundled into the service.

f17_cellular_and_5g_support.quote: With the higher throughputs provided by CAT18 LTE and 5G, wireless WAN connections become feasible as primary transports for different use cases.
f17_cellular_and_5g_support.note: Both primary and failover cellular use are evidenced. The same datasheet covers integrated and external modem options: "Based on a specific branch's direct line of sight and cellular coverage, this solution provides the flexibility of either using integrated PIM module or an external gateway. The integrated module can work in tandem with a cellular gateway for Active-Active redundancy." The SASE/SSE architecture guide corroborates 5G as a steerable WAN link. SIM management and signal monitoring specifically were not found as verbatim statements in the pages reviewed, so those two sub-elements are unevidenced even though the overall grade holds.

f19_public_cloud_gateways.quote: Cisco Secure Connect services operate in the Cisco Umbrella global cloud architecture which is network of data centers located throughout the world interconnected with a high speed, low latency backbone.
f19_public_cloud_gateways.note: Yes rather than partner_integrated. This is Cisco's own service infrastructure, not a third party's PoPs that Cisco resells: Cisco owns and operates the Umbrella global cloud architecture, publishes its data centre list, and enforces security and delivers remote access from it. Corroborated by the Umbrella global network page, "The Cisco Umbrella global cloud architecture serves more than 30,000 customers daily in 190+ countries." AWS, Azure and GCP connectivity was disregarded as it does not meet the definition.

f20_private_pops_dedicated_pops.note: Not found in public sources reviewed. Looked at the Cisco Secure Connect data centre list documentation, the Umbrella global network and data centre page, the Umbrella global cloud architecture page and the Cisco SASE/SSE architecture guide. All describe shared multi-tenant Cisco locations only. No customer-hosted, dedicated or sovereign PoP option was named on any of them. Note that the Secure Access offer description does mention that "Data center(s) located in mainland China, when and if available, require a separate subscription", but a separately subscribed regional data centre is not the same as a dedicated or sovereign PoP, so it was not treated as evidence. Unknown here means not found, not absent.

f21_private_global_backbone.quote: Cisco Secure Connect services operate in the Cisco Umbrella global cloud architecture which is network of data centers located throughout the world interconnected with a high speed, low latency backbone.
f21_private_global_backbone.note: Partial rather than yes. A global, not national, footprint is clearly evidenced and the documentation states the data centres are interconnected by a backbone. What is not evidenced is the ownership or control test in the definition: no page reviewed states that Cisco owns or controls that backbone rather than buying transit or leased capacity. The Umbrella global cloud architecture page instead emphasises internet peering and anycast, "Umbrella peers directly with more than 1000 organizations", which points towards an internet-peering-centric design. Graded partial on the ownership gap. See conflicts.

f26_sla_backed_service_fabric.quote: Cisco will use commercially reasonable efforts to deliver the Core Services to meet or exceed 99.999% Availability in accordance with the Secure Access Service Level Agreement ("SLA")
f26_sla_backed_service_fabric.note: Partial rather than yes on two grounds. First, the commitment is framed as "commercially reasonable efforts" rather than a firm contractual guarantee. Second, the definition requires commitments covering uptime, response and change handling, and only uptime was found; the offer description states the SLA terms themselves are available from a Cisco account representative or authorised partner, so response times, credits and change handling could not be read. Latency, jitter and loss commitments were not found either.

f27_integrated_next_generation_firewall.quote: FWaaS provides cloud delivered firewall services without the need to deploy, maintain, and upgrade physical or virtual appliances at a site.
f27_integrated_next_generation_firewall.note: Yes and native, not partner_integrated. The firewall is built into the Cisco Secure Access platform rather than supplied as a separate appliance or as a third party's technology. Intrusion prevention uses Cisco's own Snort engine, per the Secure Access datasheet: "Customizable IPS profiles with Snort 3.0 support." The SASE design guide confirms the pairing: "Evaluation through Secure Access FWaaS also enables Intrusion Prevention System (IPS) inspection." URL filtering and anti-malware inspection are described in the architecture guide, and DLP is graded separately.

f33_data_loss_prevention.quote: Enterprise Data Loss Prevention (DLP) provides visibility and control over sensitive data leaving your organization.
f33_data_loss_prevention.note: Native Cisco capability within Secure Access. Classification depth is corroborated on the same datasheet, "1,200+ built-in global identifiers for Personally Identifiable Information (PII), spanning 77 countries", and the SASE design guide confirms DLP is applied inline to traffic alongside SWG. Alerting and exception workflows specifically were not found as verbatim statements in the pages reviewed, so that sub-element is unevidenced, though the core classify, inspect and block requirement is clearly met.

f40_managed_service_assurance.quote: Tap into 24/7 support and escalation process for complex issues
f40_managed_service_assurance.note: Not_primary rather than yes. Round-the-clock support and an escalation path exist, but the quote is Cisco offering that to MSPs so that the MSP can assure its own customers. No page reviewed describes a Cisco-run customer-facing NOC and SOC that proactively monitors the customer's service, owns incidents through to root cause analysis, and runs structured service reviews and change governance. The Cisco Support page carries no NOC, SOC, root cause or service review language at all. In the Cisco model this assurance role generally sits with the partner or MSP.

delivery_model.quote: Cisco will use commercially reasonable efforts to deliver the Core Services to meet or exceed 99.999% Availability in accordance with the Secure Access Service Level Agreement ("SLA")
delivery_model.note: Cisco authors the SD-WAN and SSE technology (Catalyst SD-WAN, Meraki, Secure Access) and additionally operates Secure Access as its own cloud service under a contractual SLA, which is a service-operator role. Day to day managed WAN operations are largely delivered by Cisco partners and MSPs rather than by Cisco itself, per the Meraki MSP page which invites partners to "Create a multitude of offers from managed business Wi-Fi to managed SD-WAN".

underlay_ownership.quote: Route traffic across different links (MPLS, Internet, 5G, etc.) based on destination
underlay_ownership.note: Cisco is a technology vendor for the WAN edge and does not sell the physical circuits. Its architecture guide treats MPLS, internet and cellular as transports the customer already has, and the Catalyst 8300 datasheet describes terminating those links rather than providing them. No circuit, access or carrier service offering was found on any page reviewed. Graded medium confidence because the evidence is the consistent absence of a circuit offer plus transport-agnostic framing, rather than an explicit Cisco statement that it never supplies access. This is separate from the Umbrella cloud PoP estate, which Cisco does operate.

sse_layer_ownership.quote: Simplify the complexity of IT by leveraging one powerful platform for Cisco SD-WAN, SWG, ZTNA, DNS-layer security, CASB, and more.
sse_layer_ownership.note: Cisco built and owns its security service edge stack. Secure Access and Umbrella are Cisco products running on Cisco-operated data centres, the IPS engine is Cisco's own Snort 3.0, and DLP, SWG, ZTNA, CASB and FWaaS are all delivered from the same Cisco platform. There is no third-party security vendor being resold or OEM'd here, so this is native rather than partner or resold. No partner vendor to name.

regulatory_documentation.quote: Data centers are certified by industry-recognized standards such as ISO 9001:2008, ISO 27001, PCI DSS, SSAE16, and ISAE 3402
regulatory_documentation.note: Frameworks found named in body text: ISO 27001, PCI DSS, ISO 9001:2008, SSAE16, ISAE 3402, and GDPR is discussed separately on the same page. Frameworks NOT found named on any page reviewed: SOC 2, NHS DSPT, DORA, NIS2. Two caveats. First, the quote is from the Meraki trust page and covers Meraki data centres, not the whole Cisco SASE and SD-WAN estate. Second, the Cisco Trust Center compliance page surfaces SOC, ISO, FedRAMP, CSA STAR, C5, IRAP and HIPAA only as navigation link parameters behind the gated Trust Portal, not as body-text statements, so it could not carry a quote. Confidence medium for those reasons.

pop_count.note: Not found in public sources reviewed. Cisco publishes locations but not a headline count. The Cisco Secure Connect data centre documentation lists roughly 33 named locations across the Americas, APAC, Europe and MEA in a table, and the Umbrella global network page tabulates approximately 50 or more data centre locations with operators and peering fabrics, but neither page contains any sentence stating a number, so no quote is available and the count cannot be graded. The Umbrella global cloud architecture page gives reach and peering figures instead, and the Umbrella global network page states "The Cisco Umbrella global cloud architecture serves more than 30,000 customers daily in 190+ countries.", but neither is a PoP count. The two Cisco tables also differ in scope, so deriving a single figure would mean resolving that conflict myself, which is out of scope.

sla_availability_pct.quote: Cisco will use commercially reasonable efforts to deliver the Core Services to meet or exceed 99.999% Availability in accordance with the Secure Access Service Level Agreement ("SLA")
sla_availability_pct.note: Figure taken from Cisco's own contractual offer description for Secure Access, which is the strongest available source. Read the qualifier carefully: the target is 99.999% but the obligation is expressed as commercially reasonable efforts, and the underlying SLA document with its credits and measurement method is not public. Cisco separately claims historical achievement on the Umbrella marketing page, "Umbrella's DNS security services have delivered 99.999% business uptime since 2006.", which is a track record claim rather than a commitment. The figure applies to Secure Access core services; no equivalent published availability percentage was found for the SD-WAN products themselves.

sectors.healthcare.quote: Healthcare organizations run thousands of branches throughout the world, ranging from small clinic to large hospitals spanning across multiple regions.
sectors.healthcare.note: Graded on a published, healthcare-specific Cisco Validated Profile for SD-WAN, which is a dedicated sector framework rather than a passing mention. Caveat worth recording: no named healthcare customer with an SD-WAN deployment was found. Cisco's healthcare case studies (Barts Health NHS Trust, Rush University System for Health, University Hospital Frankfurt, Clarke County Hospital) are LAN, data centre or security deployments in the material read, not SD-WAN.

sectors.financial_services.quote: Argentine bank establishes a new standard for software-defined networking across global locations.
sectors.financial_services.note: BBVA is a named customer carrying Cisco's own Financial Services industry label, with Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN explicitly in the deployed products list. Banco do Brasil, Fiserv and Jammu & Kashmir Bank are further published financial services customers, though SD-WAN was not confirmed in their product lists.

sectors.retail_ecommerce.quote: As big box stores, QSRs and grocery stores rapidly adopt a cloud-first strategy, the IT landscape has become significantly different.
sectors.retail_ecommerce.note: Strongest sector evidence in the set. Cisco publishes a dedicated retail SD-WAN page and a named retail customer, Room & Board, whose case study carries the Retail industry label and lists Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN plus Meraki MX security and SD-WAN appliances.

sectors.manufacturing.quote: Kamstrup optimized its network with Cisco SD-WAN and ThousandEyes, enabling seamless global expansion.
sectors.manufacturing.note: Kamstrup's case study carries Cisco's own Manufacturing industry label and lists Cisco SD-WAN and Cisco SD-WAN Manager. Coca-Cola Icecek, Nestle and The Sto Group are further named SD-WAN customers in manufacturing or food and beverage production.

sectors.energy_utilities.quote: fleets, oil and gas, energy and water utilities, and remote condition monitoring and control
sectors.energy_utilities.note: Deliberately held at partial. Cisco's SD-WAN industrial solution brief names energy and water utilities, oil and gas and the utility grid as target use cases, but names no customer in any of them. Cisco's general energy and utilities case studies (ScottishPower Renewables, CPFL Energia, Noida Power) were checked and none was confirmed as an SD-WAN deployment in the material read. Kamstrup serves utilities but is itself labelled Manufacturing by Cisco.

sectors.government_public_sector.quote: Federal, state, and local government agencies can deploy a FedRAMP-authorized SD-WAN cloud-delivered solution designed to optimize performance, enhance security, and simplify their operations.
sectors.government_public_sector.note: Two independent supports: a published accreditation claim (FedRAMP authorisation for the cloud-delivered SD-WAN solution) and a named public sector customer, Buckinghamshire Council, whose entry lists Cisco Software-Defined Wide Area Network.

sectors.education.quote: As schools, colleges, and universities rapidly adopt a cloud-first strategy, the IT landscape has become significantly different.
sectors.education.note: Graded yes on a dedicated Cisco SD-WAN page for education, which meets the dedicated industry page test. Confidence held at medium because no named education customer with an SD-WAN deployment was found: the leading Cisco education networking story, West Ada School District, is a Meraki and Catalyst LAN and wireless deployment with no SD-WAN component.

sectors.transport_logistics.quote: United Airlines uses Cisco SD-WAN to centralize network management, enhance security, and boost performance across its global operations.
sectors.transport_logistics.note: United Airlines is a named SD-WAN customer promoted on the SD-WAN solution page itself. The SD-WAN industrial solution brief separately names transit, rail, trucking and service fleets. Cisco's wider transportation roster (DP World, easyJet, Alcoa ports) was checked but SD-WAN was not confirmed in those product lists.

sectors.professional_services.quote: Tech Mahindra reimagines network operations to deliver agility across 32 branches and 6 hubs.
sectors.professional_services.note: Tech Mahindra's case study carries Cisco's own Professional Services industry label and is headlined on SD-WAN, listing Cisco Software-Defined WAN (SD-WAN) and Cisco vManage. Worth noting Tech Mahindra is an IT services firm and also a Cisco channel partner, so it is a less neutral reference than a pure end customer.

sectors.hospitality_leisure.quote: Meraki MX security and SD-WAN appliances
sectors.hospitality_leisure.note: Distinctive Resorts is a named case study carrying Cisco's own Hospitality industry label with Meraki MX security and SD-WAN appliances in the deployed products list. Confidence held at medium because the story is headlined on smart cameras and the SD-WAN element is incidental rather than the subject. Cisco's Meraki hospitality roster is large (InterContinental Hotels Group, Club Mediterranee, Motel 6, bluegr Hotels) but that index page does not state which of them use MX SD-WAN.

regions.uk_ireland.note: Cisco Secure Access publishes three separate UK and Ireland edge locations: London (peering LINX / LoNAP), Manchester (peering LINX Manchester) and Dublin (peering INEX), all listed as Cisco Edge v1. Corroborated by the Secure Connect data centre list, which shows London UK. A UK public sector SD-WAN customer (Buckinghamshire Council) is also published.

regions.europe.note: Extensive published mainland European footprint in the Secure Access regions table: Frankfurt and Dusseldorf (DE-CIX), Amsterdam (AMS-IX), Paris and Marseille, Milan, Madrid, Stockholm, Copenhagen, Prague, Warsaw, Bucharest and Zurich. Corroborated by the Secure Connect data centre list.

regions.north_america.note: Dense published US and Canadian footprint. US locations include Ashburn (Equinix Ashburn), New York (NYIIX) and Los Angeles (Equinix Los Angeles); Canadian locations include Toronto (TorIX), Vancouver and Alberta and Quebec multi-availability-zone regions. FedRAMP authorisation is also published for US government.

regions.asia_pacific.note: Published locations across Singapore, Japan (Tokyo and Osaka), India (Mumbai, Chennai, Hyderabad), South Korea (Seoul), Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia (Jakarta) and Australia (Sydney via Equinix Sydney / MegaIX, and Melbourne). Corroborated by the Secure Connect data centre list.

regions.middle_east_africa.note: Published Middle East locations include Dubai (UAE-IX), Bahrain, Tel Aviv, Jeddah and Riyadh. Published African locations include Johannesburg (NAPAfrica IX) and Cape Town. The Secure Connect list flags Johannesburg as partially available for one service, so coverage depth varies by component even though presence is clearly published.

regions.latin_america.note: Published locations include Sao Paulo (IX.br Sao Paulo) and Rio de Janeiro in Brazil, plus Queretaro and a Mexico Central multi-availability-zone region. BBVA, a published Catalyst SD-WAN customer, is described as operating across Europe and Latin America.

regions.china_mainland.note: Cisco does publish mainland China entries, listed under Asia / China as Beijing (Multi-AZ) and Ningxia (Multi-AZ). Graded partial rather than yes for three reasons recorded here rather than resolved: both are AWS public cloud regions rather than Cisco Edge points of presence, Ningxia is marked as by-request rather than on-demand, and both carry a footnote marker whose conditions were not read. Note the disagreement between sources: the Cisco Secure Connect data centre list (evidence 5) shows only Hong Kong under the China heading and no mainland location at all. Cisco publishes nothing in either source about the licensed arrangement required to operate in mainland China.

organisation_fit.large_global_enterprise.quote: scaling connectivity across 1700 sites in 185 countries through a unified platform
organisation_fit.large_global_enterprise.note: Unambiguous. The SD-WAN solution page leads with global enterprise references (Nestle across 1700 sites in 185 countries, United Airlines global operations, BBVA across more than 25 countries). This is the segment Cisco puts front and centre for Catalyst SD-WAN.

organisation_fit.mid_market.quote: Cisco small and medium enterprise solutions
organisation_fit.mid_market.note: Cisco runs a dedicated small and medium enterprise segment page, and the Meraki MX line (cloud-managed security and SD-WAN) is the vehicle for this segment, appearing in mid-sized customer stories such as Distinctive Resorts and Room & Board. Confidence held at medium because the SME segment page itself does not name SD-WAN, so the mid-market claim is inferred from the Meraki product line rather than stated as SD-WAN targeting.

organisation_fit.small_business.quote: Gartner characterizes the SD-WAN small branch as a remote site supporting up to 10 people, where simplicity, cost consciousness, and flexibility of transport choices are key.
organisation_fit.small_business.note: Graded partial deliberately. Cisco addresses small organisations corporately, and it publishes a small branch SD-WAN validated design, but that design describes small sites within a 500-site chain, not a small business as the buyer. No pricing, packaging or case study aimed at a standalone small business SD-WAN buyer was found. The two Meraki pages that would most likely settle this (evidence 25 and 26) were blocked by robots.txt.

published_pricing.note: No price is published that we could quote. The value_tier field on this record is a Netify assessment of relative cost position, not a supplier claim.

conflicts.claim_a: Cisco Secure Connect and Umbrella data centres worldwide are "interconnected with a high speed, low latency backbone", implying a vendor-controlled inter-PoP network.
conflicts.claim_b: The Umbrella global cloud architecture page attributes inter-region performance to internet peering and anycast rather than to a backbone, stating "Umbrella peers directly with more than 1000 organizations" and that "Our innovative use of Anycast augmented routing is integral to Cisco Umbrella's top performance and rock-solid reliability".

conflicts.claim_a: Contractual offer description frames 99.999% as a commercially reasonable efforts target: "Cisco will use commercially reasonable efforts to deliver the Core Services to meet or exceed 99.999% Availability".
conflicts.claim_b: Umbrella marketing page presents 99.999% as achieved historical fact: "Umbrella's DNS security services have delivered 99.999% business uptime since 2006."

conflicts.claim_a: Cisco Secure Connect data centre documentation tabulates roughly 33 named service locations, with some marked TBD or Coming.
conflicts.claim_b: The Umbrella global network and traffic page tabulates a materially larger estate, on the order of 50 or more data centre locations.
